text_translated_detailed: Register of Such Papers Which Today Were Sent to Batavia with the Ship Groenswaard [Greenfield]; Consigned to His High Nobility the Well-Esteemed, Greatly Honored Lord Adriaan Valkenier, Governor General, together with the Well-Esteemed Lords Councillors of Dutch India. No. 1. Original letter from the Head and Council of this Office to their High Noble and Greatly Honored the High Indian Government at Batavia. No. 2. Secret letter likewise signed by the Head alone, to the same as written above, under today's date. No. 3. Copy thereof, dated 20 April of the current year, to and from the same as before. No. 4. Daily register kept at this Office from 15 January 1737 to 23 January 1738. No. 5. A report, together with a certificate from Siam dated 25 January of the year 1738, and five packing letters concerning shortages found in five packages of hamans [uncertain: possibly a textile or commodity]. No. 6. Original request for supplies, both for the Offices of Siam and Ligoor [Ligor], as well as for the King and the Bercq [uncertain: possibly a title or position], for the years 1738 to 3/39. No. 7. Two sets of copies of the trading journal, large and cash books, for Siam and Ligoor for the years 17 to 23/37. No. 8. Six sets of copies of salary, provisions, and journal books from Siam and Ligoor for the years 17 to 9/47. No. 9. Two general accounts of this Office, under the last day of February and the last day of August of the current year. No. 10. One cost accounting of the unavoidable provisions supplied to this vessel. No. 11. A bundle of outgoing and incoming letters to and from the Office of Ligoor from 14 February to 14 September of the current year. No. 12. An original resolution taken upon closing the books under the last day of August. No. 13. A bundle of samples of various Persian and Surat fabrics. No. 14. Two boxes with models of Siamese pagodas from Siam dated 25 January of the year 1733, in order that they might, if possible, be reproduced in glass. No. 15. A

text_translated_detailed: From Siam On the 25th January A:o 1738 Batavia To his High Excellency The Well Noble Great honorable Lord Adriaan Valckenier Governor General, together with The Well Noble Lords Council of Dutch India High Esteemed Excellency, great Honorable: Mighty Well-wise, Foreseeing Most generous Lords - High Commanding Lords In accordance with your well noble high honorable much esteemed order it is proper with all humble Respect to communicate that we this vessel both on its arrival and departure have had properly inspected by commissioners, and in the same for so far as it has come to their attention no private goods have been discovered, moreover as such deep going has been found your well noble high honorable by the enclosed reports to us thereupon delivered, and these in authentic copies are accompanying, it will come to light, Whereby we hope your well noble high honorable much esteemed order in this to have fulfilled and remain with humble Respect /:understood:/ High Commanding Lords /:lower:/ your: well noble High honorable humble and lowly Servants /:signed:/ Theodorus Siam On the 25th January A:o 1738 From I:b van den Heuvel, W:m De Glij, N:s Bang /:in margin/ Siam in the N:ts Comptoir India On the 25th January A:o 1738. Report to the Honored Honored Lord Theodorus Iacobus van den Heuvel Merchant and chief over the Trade of the Honored Company: together with the Council Esteemed foreseeing and most Discreet By your Honored Excellencies' order and sent out after this roadstead to properly inspect the ship Groenswaerd so it is proper thereupon with Respect that we undersigned after having performed this for so far as we have been able to discover, have found no private goods in said vessel, and on its arrival at this roadstead is deep going for thirteen and one half and behind fourteen and one quarter feet, with which and other we believe to your Honored Excellencies' esteemed command fully to have fulfilled

text_translated_detailed: Having been sent to this roadstead to properly inspect the ship Groenswaerd, we the undersigned respectfully report that, after having carried out this inspection to the extent we were able to determine, we found no private goods in the aforementioned vessel, and upon its arrival at this roadstead it drew forward thirteen and one-half feet and aft fourteen and one-quarter feet. With this and all other matters, we believe we have fully satisfied your Excellencies' esteemed commands, and we remain in expectation thereof with great respect, earnestly and very discreetly your Excellencies' obedient servants, signed W.m D' Ghij and F.s van Essen, at the side. At the roadstead Siam on the 3rd of October in the year 1737. Report to the Esteemed Gentlemen Theodorus Jacobus van den Heuvel, merchant and chief over the trade of the Esteemed Company, together with the Council. Earnestly and very discreetly. Having been ordered by your Excellencies and sent to this roadstead to properly inspect the ship Groenswaerd, we the undersigned respectfully report that, after having carried out this inspection to the extent we were able to determine, we found no private goods in the aforementioned vessel, and upon its departure from this roadstead it drew forward fifteen feet and aft seventeen feet. With this and all other matters, we believe we have fully satisfied your Excellencies' esteemed commands, and we remain in expectation thereof with great respect, earnestly and very discreetly your Excellencies' obedient servants, signed W.m d' Ghij and F.s van Essen, at the side. At the roadstead Siam on the 4th of February in the year 1738.

Declaration concerning the matter that occurred between the Under-Merchant and Resident at this Office Jan Christoffel Werlit, on the one hand, and the bookkeeper and Second [in command] Willem Meijboom, on the other hand.

We, the undersigned, Cornelis Loots, Paulus Scheeper, from Siam under date of the 25th of January in the year 1738, and Guillaume Teisseire, declare by these [presents] in place of an oath, at the request and petition of the Under-Merchant and Resident at this Office Johan Christoffel Werlix, that he, the petitioner, requested the Bookkeeper and Second here, Willem Meijboom, at his house, where we deponents were then present, to provide the copy of the letter which the aforementioned Second had written in the year [17]37 to the charge of the Petitioner, to the Chief and Council in Siam; whereupon the said Second, in our presence, answered the petitioner that he could not produce it, since the same copy, written by him, was sought and could not be found to be handed over to the petitioner. All of which aforesaid we deponents declare to be the pure truth, giving as reason for our knowledge that we were present thereat, and we further testify nothing, presenting the same at all times, if needed, to be confirmed with an oath. Thus passed, given and signed by us below. Undersigned: In the Dutch Office Ligoor, the 21st of May in the year 1737. And was signed: C. Loots, assistant; P. Scheeper, Under-Steersman and Pro. Seisseire, third Master. Below: Agrees. Was signed: W. Meijboom. From Siam under date of the 25th.

We, the undersigned, Cornelis Loots, Paulus Scheeper, from Siam under date of the 25th of January in the year 1738, and Guillaume Teisseire, declare by these presents in place of an oath, at the request and petition of the Under-Merchant and Resident at this Office Johan Christoffel Werlix, that he, the petitioner, requested the Bookkeeper and Second here, Willem Meijboom, at his house, where we deponents were then present, to provide the copy of the letter which the aforementioned Second had written in the year 1737 to the charge of the Petitioner, to the Chief and Council in Siam; whereupon the said Second, in our presence, answered the petitioner that he could not produce it, since the same copy, written by him, was sought and could not be found to be handed over to the petitioner. All of which aforesaid we deponents declare to be the pure truth, giving as reason for our knowledge that we were present thereat, and we further testify nothing, presenting the same at all times, if needed, to be confirmed with an oath. Thus passed, given and signed by us below. Undersigned: In the Dutch Office Ligoor, the 21st of May in the year 1737. And was signed: C. Loots, assistant; P. Scheeper, Under-Steersman and Pro. Seisseire, third Master. Below: Agrees. Was signed: W. Meijboom. From Siam under date of the 25th.

text_translated_detailed: From Siam Under date 25th January 1738. /. Translation Siamese Writing sent by the New Governor Pra Sombatiboen in the Lodge, the 23rd of June 1737. /. The Caloeang stick new Wisit makes known by the Toek, that he has received the written answer from the old sija and has made it known to the new Governor, whereupon the new Governor states that there is an order from the Lord Berquelang to the Governor's Council, which forbids that the Resident in the Land of Ligoor and the districts subordinate thereto may not purchase any tin, nor any single rank [uncertain: possibly a measure or grade of tin] for the time being, and that if any inhabitant secretly sells tin to the Company and is caught, he shall be punished forthwith; it also appears clearly from the Translation of the Lord Bercquelang that the tin of this year is not for the account of the E[steemed] Company, for which reason in the release of the tin now held, no notice was given to the Captain of the Dutch there; but the Captain had the same brought in and stored in the Lodge, although the Chinese, who had the said tin, said that it was from the new Governor, so the Captain did not believe the Chinese. From Siam Under date 25th January A.D. 1738. /. text_translated_detailed: From the esteemed [person] of Siam, dated 25 January, year 1738. The courtesies and much gentler treatment as before, now noticing that the ball has been missed and wanting everything, will lose everything, all remorse over this deed seems to have been done, and the answers thereupon will be obtained shortly. You will be able to discern this well from the letter to the high Indian Government now in flying seal being passed to you, so that after the attachment of a bill of lading and invoice of the two hundred bahar of tin [a unit of weight] which the King has granted and must be loaded into the small boat, it will be closed and sealed as is proper. It appears that for the arrival of the ships there is no prospect of restoring the previous trade, inasmuch as these two hundred bahar, of which a very sharp [uncertain: original text] now passes for its worthy satisfaction, must be sent without money, since, although [we] have pressed hard on this matter, no final answer has been obtained, and it seems to us as if the King wishes to validate this in place of the outstanding Company's monies, regarding which there has also been enough struggle, and we could also have obtained a [uncertain: original text] to have it restituted in cash. From Siam, dated 25 January, year 1738. Yet we have thought it now that matters have begun to turn somewhat more in our favor, better to be and to accord more with the Company's interest, to let the same continue to run and to hold in status until the arrival of the ships, rather than for that bare pen, without the least interest, notwithstanding that they have been outstanding so long, to have to receive and accept again. But if and when the Calouanger Pra Sambatiban, now with you, whose greedy, quarrelsome and irritable temperament is fully known to us, and therefore also causes us to approve the 90 guilders [modern equivalent: Dutch currency] granted to him,

text_translated_detailed: From Siam under date 25 January in the year 1738 Monday the 16th of December in the year 1737 Present: the Merchant Theodorus Jacobus van den Heuvel, upper merchant, the under-merchant Willem D'Glij, second, and the assistant Nicolaas Bang, soldier, bookkeeper. Given that the ship "The Land of Promise" [normalized version: 't Land van belofte] arrived only on the 7th of this month at this comptoir, and its officers did not arrive here earlier, and for this reason the goods which were sent by their Honors as a gift to the king and the regent were delivered on the 11th thereof, by which means, and also by the slow manner of this land, no report could be received of the prince's and regent's return gift. Therefore the head of the comptoir presents for consideration in the head of this document whether it would not be necessary to charge these goods, as in previous years, to the account of outstanding accounts, in order that after receiving notice of the aforesaid prince's and regent's return gift at the rate thereof to be relieved thereof again. And since all necessary entries and write-offs, together with the expenses of the comptoir Ligoor, had already been included in the most recent account books, in order to proceed as quickly as possible with closing the aforesaid books and with summarizing all the expenses and profits for the year ahead, in order to be able to send them with the first departing vessel. This being unanimously approved, upon examination of the expenses and profits, they were found in comparison with the most recently passed year as follows, namely: The general expenses of the accounting year 1736 amounted to ƒ 316,008 [modern equivalent: guilders]; the same for 1737 amounted to ƒ 145,312:4:—, by which means this accounting year had greater expenses than the year past by ƒ 7,051:7:8. The aforesaid increased expenses and decreased profits, when compared with each other, show that at both comptoirs Siam and Ligoor this most recent accounting year in comparison with the year past, one has fallen behind by a sum of ƒ 9,794:1:—

text_translated_detailed: received by way of the Land of Promises on the 2nd of April 1738 From Siam On the 25th of January in the year 1738 Batavia To His High Excellency The Well-Born, greatly esteemed: Lord Adriaan Valckenier Governor General, together with The Well-Born Gentlemen Councillors of the Netherlands Indies High and Noble, Most Esteemed, greatly esteemed: valiant, wise, foresighted and most generous Commanding Lords, considering that the lord Bereque Lang immediately after the papers were already closed sent a letter to be dispatched privately and not among the Company's official papers to Surat: and the undersigned has been informed that the aforementioned letter's contents consist principally of great promises and an offer of toll exemptions for the Surat merchants, who have not been here for two years, and who have abandoned this land on account of the dreadful extortions committed against them, in order to entice and attract them back here again, which would be entirely disadvantageous for the Company and would disturb the trade here. Therefore he takes the liberty to humbly present this to Your High Excellency by means of this letter, so that the same, once opened and translated, may be /that one here did not dare to undertake nor entrust to anyone/: Your High Excellency may discover not only the truth here, but also the inner disposition of the king, by whose express order it was prepared, and likewise may take such measures as Your High Excellency shall find to be appropriate. — but I humbly request that in the forthcoming letter to the Bereque Lang you will be pleased to write that this letter has been sent forward so that the undersigned may remain in confidence and credit with him. — meanwhile with the deepest respect is /understood:/ High and Noble, Most Esteemed, greatly esteemed: valiant, wise, foresighted and most generous commanding Lords /lower:/ Your High Excellency's humble and obedient Servant /was signed:/ J„s I:bs van den Heuvel /in

At present, I am dispatching and sending by the Company's ship to Batavia the persons of Choen Tjapasientoel and Choen Siesoer Tib, horse handlers, as well as Moen Moera-at and Pantoeng, horse doctors. I request that a money loan be granted to these same persons according to custom, and that these people be transported with a letter of introduction on Java's Company ship, and that they be informed of the places or villages where many horses are available so that such may be purchased by them as will be needed.
